relations.note: Velnias hides in stones, trees, water, animals, or clothing while Perkūnas attacks.
relations.source: Lithuanian belief legends published by Vėlius

relations.note: Latvian folklore associates thunder with Pērkons pursuing Velns or another evil being.

relations.myth: God and Velnias create the world
relations.note: Velnias accompanies God, retrieves primordial earth, and shares creative labor.
Velnias hides some retrieved earth in his mouth, attempting to appropriate it from God.

relations.myth: Opposed creation of animals and landscape
relations.note: Velnias imitates God’s creations, producing harmful creatures and uneven or barren terrain.

relations.myth: God banishes or punishes the devil
relations.note: Christian God commands, punishes, outwits, or banishes Velnias in catechesis and folklore.
Christ or a wandering divine figure defeats, exposes, or corrects Velnias.
Mary’s holy name, signs, or prayers drive Velnias away in folk-Christian belief.
Saints and their holy names or signs repel Velnias in Christianized legends.
Scholars compare or equate Velnias with the Slavic cattle and chthonic god Veles.
Later scholarship disputes whether Łasicki’s god of souls Vielona is Velnias.
Modern authors equate this Old Prussian underworld-associated figure with Velnias.
Later reconstruction identifies Grunau’s death-associated Patollo as an Old Prussian Velnias equivalent.
Modern reconstructions claim Velnias abducts or possesses Aušrinė, provoking the thunder-god’s pursuit.
Greimas connected Velnias with the medieval divine smith Teliavelis, without textual identification.
Gimbutas and others compared Velnias with Odin through death, magic, horses, prophecy, and one-eyedness.
Modern comparative reconstructions present Varuṇa as an analogue or equivalent of Velnias.
